descriptor: The largest animal known to have ever lived, sustained almost entirely by tiny shrimp-like krill.

physical.fact: The largest animal known to have lived, it can eat about 6 tons of krill in a single day.

range.summary: All the major oceans, from polar feeding grounds to tropical waters, with resident groups off Sri Lanka and in the Gulf of California.

regions.name: Antarctic waters
regions.note: Antarctic blue whales fell from about 239,000 to about 360 by 1973, then began a slow recovery.

regions.name: South Georgia
regions.note: Most of the 42,698 blue whales killed at South Georgia were taken by the mid 1930s; they all but vanished.

regions.name: Gulf of Alaska
regions.note: Blue whales were caught here until whaling for them ended in 1965, then went largely unseen.

regions.name: Iceland
regions.note: Hunted off Iceland until protection in 1960, North Atlantic blue whales still feed here in summer.

regions.name: California coast
regions.note: About 2,200 blue whales feed off California, put at 97% of pre-whaling numbers by a 2014 study.

regions.name: Gulf of California
regions.note: Eastern North Pacific blue whales gather in the Gulf of California in winter and spring.

regions.name: Haida Gwaii, BC
regions.note: Blue whales seen off British Columbia from 1997 were photo-matched to the California population.

regions.name: Chiloé and Corcovado
regions.note: Surveys in 2003 found 153 blue whales, including mothers and calves, feeding off southern Chile.

regions.name: Southern Sri Lanka
regions.note: A northern Indian Ocean population stays year round off Sri Lanka instead of migrating to polar seas.

regions.name: Bonney Upwelling
regions.note: Pygmy blue whales feed in the cold upwelling off South Australia and Victoria each summer.

regions.name: South Georgia return
regions.note: A February 2020 survey logged 58 blue whale sightings, after only one in 1998 to 2018.

rangeHistory.note: Lost markers show where whaling left blue whales effectively absent, not that every whale vanished; the 2020 South Georgia return falls after the last population year.

population.unit: Antarctic blue whales (B. m. intermedia) in the Southern Ocean

source.label: Branch et al. 2004, Marine Mammal Science; Branch 2007, IDCR/SOWER circumpolar surveys

population.note: The 1904 and 1973 values are model back-estimates of the pre-whaling and lowest populations; later points are survey estimates south of 60°S. Worldwide, IUCN estimates 5,000 to 15,000 mature blue whales.

threats.title: Ship strikes
threats.detail: Collisions in busy shipping lanes off California and Sri Lanka kill whales every year.

threats.title: Ocean noise
threats.detail: Shipping and seismic surveys mask the low calls blue whales use to find each other.

threats.title: Entanglement
threats.detail: Fishing gear and lines can wrap around whales and wound or drown them.

threats.title: Shifting krill supply
threats.detail: Warming seas and krill fishing could reduce the swarms the whales need to feed.

places.name: Mirissa
places.note: Blue whales feed a few kilometres offshore, close to a busy shipping lane.

places.name: Santa Barbara Channel
places.note: A major summer feeding ground for eastern North Pacific blue whales.

places.name: Loreto, Gulf of California
places.note: Mothers and calves in calm water inside a marine national park.

places.name: Les Escoumins, St. Lawrence Estuary
places.note: North Atlantic blue whales feed on krill, sometimes seen from shore.

sightings.tip: Seasons depend on the site: December to April off Sri Lanka, February to April in the Gulf of California, and July to September off California and in the St. Lawrence.

actions.title: Back slower shipping
actions.detail: Voluntary speed limits in whale zones cut fatal strikes and also reduce underwater noise.

actions.title: Watch whales responsibly
actions.detail: Choose operators that keep their distance and never chase or cut off a whale.

actions.title: Skip krill-oil supplements
actions.detail: Antarctic krill is the main food of recovering blue whales, so plant-based omega-3 is the safer choice.

actions.title: Report sightings
actions.detail: Logging sightings in citizen science apps helps map where ships and whales overlap.

summary.text: The blue whale is a species of baleen whale and the largest marine mammal in the rorqual family Balaenopteridae. Reaching a maximum confirmed length of 29.9–30.5 m (98–100 ft) and weighing up to 190–200 t, it is the largest animal known to have ever existed. The blue whale's long and slender body can be of various shades of greyish-blue on its upper surface and somewhat lighter underneath. Four subspecies are recognized: B. m. musculus in the North Atlantic and North Pacific, B. m. intermedia in the Southern Ocean, B. m. brevicauda in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific Ocean, and B. m. indica in the Northern Indian Ocean. There is a population in the waters off Chile that may constitute a fifth subspecies.
